back: Represent $Q(s,a;\theta)$ with parameters so values generalise across states; needed when the state space is too large for a table.
Differentiate only through $Q(s,a;\theta)$; the target $y$ is treated as a constant (code: detach / stop-gradient).
Ring buffer of past transitions sampled uniformly for minibatches: decorrelates data and reuses it. Valid because Q-learning is off-policy.
A frozen copy $\theta^-$ used to compute targets, refreshed every $C$ steps; stops the target from moving with every update.
Hard: $\theta^-\leftarrow\theta$ every $C$ steps. Soft: $\theta^-\leftarrow(1-\tau)\theta^-+\tau\theta$ each step.
Function approximation + bootstrapping + off-policy data: together they can diverge.

front: Gradient of the DQN loss for linear Q
back: $\partial L/\partial W[a]=-\frac1B\sum_{i:a_i=a}\delta_i\phi(s_i)$; only rows of actions taken change.

front: What does $(1-d)$ do in the target?
back: Removes the bootstrap at terminal transitions, since a terminal state has value 0.
Select $a'=\arg\max Q(s',\cdot;\theta)$ with the online net but evaluate it with the target net, reducing overestimation from the max.
With one-hot state features linear DQN reduces to tabular Q-learning.
Keeps the scale of TD errors and gradients comparable across tasks; wrong when reward magnitude carries information.

front: How to test a DQN implementation
back: Check the gradient against finite differences with fixed target weights, and run on a tiny MDP with a known optimal $Q^*$.
